The Cervélo Soloist—The Race-Inspired Road Bike That Makes Sense for the Way Most Riders Actually Ride

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that over the last few years, many bike brands have tried to combine the benefits of their aero bike platform and climbing bikes into an all-arounder.
  • In a recent development, cervélo touts the Soloist as its do-everything road platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that over the last few years, many bike brands have tried to combine the benefits of their aero bike platform and climbing bikes into an all-arounder. When I managed a Trek store, the brand debuted the Madone Gen8. Trek intended it as the next logical step in its road bike lineup by combining the Madone’s speed with the Émonda’s low weight. Other examples of this trend include the Specialized Tarmac and Cannondale’s SuperSix Evo.

In a recent development, cervélo touts the Soloist as its do-everything road platform. While you’ll see its S5 and R5 at races like the Tour de France, the Soloist probably won’t show up at the starting line of any Grand Tours. That’s because the Cervélo-sponsored Visma-Lease a Bike team doesn’t need a third road bike; it already has race-winning aero bikes and dedicated climbing bikes for its athletes. Most days those riders use the S5, and on the steepest alpine climbs they can go with the R5.

In a recent development, but most of us don’t have the money, space, or desire to own multiple road bikes to choose between depending on the route we’re riding that day. One road bike that flies up climbs, inspires confidence on descents, and holds well in a paceline is the key for many riders. After almost three months of riding, I found Cervélo’s Soloist fits right into that sweet spot.

In a recent development, the Soloist mixes the pure speed of the S5 with the uphill float of the R5. It sits between both models in weight—about a pound heavier than the R5 and about two pounds lighter than the S5. Visually, the Soloist looks like a midpoint between both bikes. It brings the lines of the R5 while tying in the aero aesthetics of the S5, but the geometry charts paint a different picture. The Soloist leans toward the S5 when looking at the geometry charts for each model. When shopping the Cervélo lineup consider the pricing. The Ultegra Di2 model of the S5 and R5 are both listed at $10,100. The Soloist gives the benefits of each bike, and saves you almost $2,000 for the Ultegra Di2 model.

Recent findings suggest that the Soloist lineup ranges from $6,800 for the SRAM Rival AXS model up to $11,000 for the SRAM Red AXS–equipped bike. I tested the Shimano Ultegra Di2-equipped version, which sells for $8,250. This bike comes stock with a 4iii power meter, an integrated carbon bar and stem, and carbon wheels. My 54cm test bike weighed 15.9 pounds without the bottles or the pedals—pretty respectable for an aero-ish bike with Ultegra components.

Recent findings suggest that straight out of the box, it was almost ready to roll. Although Cervélo equips this bike with many parts I’d choose for my own bike, I swapped out the stock 700x29c Vittoria Corsa Next TLR G2.0 tires after only a few rides. The rubber was okay on flatter rides, but lacked the grip and ride feel I wanted on twisting descents.

Installing 28mm Pirelli P Zero TLR Race tires was exactly what the Soloist needed to elevate my confidence on descents. The tires made the bike feel locked-in when leaning into turns (I even bagged a couple of Strava trophies on our local descents).

The Soloist ships with aero bottles. Cervélo claims the bottles save 4.3 watts compared to standard round bottles. However, that savings doesn’t matter if you’re wasting energy fumbling with your bottles. The aero ones fit so tight in their cages I almost fell on my first ride trying to remove one.

Even after weeks of testing, I didn’t get used to these bidons. I’ve tried other aero bottle setups and haven’t had the same matter. Plus, the stock aero cages that come with the bike don’t pair as well with traditional round bottles as some brands’ aero cages.

It has been revealed that for my first ride, I dove right into the deep end by taking the Soloist up Fiddler’s Elbow. This notorious mile-and-a-half climb gains a little over 700 feet with grades that exceed 20 percent near its summit.

It has been revealed that I’ve done this climb at least twenty times on my Trek Madone, with gearing that is a bit more favorable for climbing than the Soloist’s 36x34t lowest gear. But even with taller gearing, the Cervélo floated up the climb. The bike’s geometry put me in a comfortable position, and I appreciated the Soloist’s lower weight on steeper parts of the climb.

But the Soloist didn’t only excel on climbs. The backside of Fiddler’s features a twisting, high-speed descent where maintaining your line is critical, and the bike felt stable. Once I reached the bottom, I had rolling farm roads back to the office, similar to where I did the bulk of my daily rides with this bike.

The Soloist shines on undulating rural roads and group rides. Sometimes our office lunch rides lean toward a spicier pace, with a single or double paceline of up to eight riders. The Soloist is calm, collected, and easy to ride in groups, and its aerodynamics helped when I started to fall off the back and had to catch back to the group.

Lastly, since you don’t always ride on butter-smooth tarmac, I also tested the Soloist on roads outside of its typical scope. The bike felt confident, even on some of the chunky gravel roads. However, I don’t recommend doing this too often with the Soloist; it doesn’t have enough tire clearance for actual gravel tread.

It has been revealed that the bike proved easy to ride and live with. I wish I didn’t have to send the Soloist back to Cervélo, as I’d gladly spend more hours on this bike.

It has been revealed that bicycling’s Test Editor, Dan Chabanov, felt like the previous model tried to mix the benefits of the R5 and S5, but missed the mark. “I found it pretty unremarkable. Not in a bad way, but compared to other bikes at the time it just kind of split everything down the middle. It wasn’t very aero but it was aero-ish. It wasn’t very light, but it wasn’t overly heavy. It did a lot of stuff well, but it never really wowed me,” says Chabanov.

It has been revealed that the new model irons out those wrinkles. Cervélo shaved nearly a pound off the Ultegra model and added more aero features from the S5—notably the integrated handlebar and stem combination.

It has been revealed that I’m impressed after a few months using the new-generation Soloist as my primary road bike. It climbs better than other comparable bikes I’ve tried, holds a pocket in a paceline well, and descends like a banshee. Many brands have tried to blend the watt savings of an aero bike and the weight of a climbing bike. Cervélo took a swing with the previous Soloist model, but refined the previous generation to create a well-blended machine.

Recent findings suggest that this bike is the great choice for everyone from the local crit ripper to the Saturday coffee shop ride champion. If you get this bike, then pick up a pair of Pirelli P Zero Race tires or Continental GP 5000 tires to unlock its full potential. This bike is at the top of my list for those of us who want to have one road bike at home that can rip every ride.

Recent findings suggest that jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#56773. What Yoga Can Teach You About Quieting Your Thoughts

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1856 w)

What Yoga Can Teach You About Quieting Your Thoughts

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s one thing to practice yoga and to think maybe you’ll try meditation one of these times.
  • In order to embrace meditation, I found it incredibly helpful to study yoga philosophy and try to understand why I’m practicing.
  • Industry observers note that the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is generally considered the primary source for yoga philosophy, although some scholars question how this came to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s one thing to practice yoga and to think maybe you’ll try meditation one of these times. It’s another to understand how these practices can support you in everyday life. In his latest book, accessible yoga teacher and YJ contributor Jivana Heyman explains the connection among yoga, meditation, and how you navigate your days. Although books explaining poses and esoteric theories abound, Heyman’s Yoga Meditation: Finding a Path Back to Your Self explains how these apply to any situation through storytelling, relatable examples, and insightful questions you can contemplate or rely on as journal prompts. The following excerpt helps you understand the connection so you can begin to try it in your own life.—Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ.

In order to embrace meditation, I found it incredibly helpful to study yoga philosophy and try to understand why I’m practicing. I realize that many people find philosophy boring, but I always recommend that my students begin meditation with some understanding of the philosophical concepts behind the practice.

Industry observers note that the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali is generally considered the primary source for yoga philosophy, although some scholars question how this came to be. There is also a debate among scholars about the date of the text, which may be anywhere from 2200 to 1500 years old. Personally, I think the Sutras have staying power because Patanjali consolidated thousands of years of teachings into a relatively terse collection of 196 incredibly insightful aphorisms.

The reason I love starting our meditation conversation with the Sutras is that it offers much insight into how the mind works, as well as how to use yoga to work with the mind. His main goal is to teach us to quiet our mind so that we can experience the eternal true Self, or spirit.

Yoga is a process of remembering who we really are and what Patanjali does, in a variety of ways, is show us how to do just that. We don’t need to become something else or earn enlightenment. In fact, my favorite thing about the Sutras is that he starts with the positive assumption that we are spirit and the recognition that our spiritual nature has been obscured by the mind’s attachments and desires. In other words, there’s nothing to gain, just a lot to release.

In the very beginning of the Sutras, Patanjali offers what is considered the definition of yoga: “Yogah chitta vritti nirodhah.” (1.2) which is often translated as, “Yoga is the stilling of the changing states of the mind.” 20 It is a surprising statement because he’s saying that quieting the thoughts and emotions in the mind is both the practice of yoga and the state of yoga—union with the true self.

So right off the bat, Patanjali is already talking about the practice of meditation and working with the mind. In the next Sutra, he goes on to say that, “When that is accomplished, the Seer abides in its own true nature.” (1.3) 21 In other words, when the mind quiets down and you find stillness, you experience peace, joy, and bliss—whatever words you’d like to use for the experience of your divinity.

According to Patanjali, the process of quieting the mind begins with concentration, which is at the heart of meditation. He’s open-minded about what we’re concentrating on. Instead, he emphasizes the process of concentration. He explains that you can remove the obstacles to the experience of yoga, “By meditating on anything one chooses that is elevating.” (1.39) 22.

According to recent reports, consciously working to quiet the mind is a theme throughout his treatise on yoga. In other words, the entirety of the text is basically about meditation. He goes on to expound on the contents of the mind, the obstacles to practice, how to avoid suffering, and eventually he describes the eight limbs of yoga, which is essentially a detailed meditation program.

There’s a reason Patanjali devotes the Sutras to working with the mind. Because of the nature of the mind, as well as our noisy culture, we seem to have a distorted understanding of ourselves. We have identified with our body and mind, yet these are the parts of us that are always changing. Instead, Patanjali is asking us to identify with the part that is eternal—our unchanging spirit.

Sources indicate that it’s also interesting to consider how asana (yoga poses) is considered in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. In this text, asana doesn’t simply lead us to meditation, it is meditation. People often recite Patanjali’s definition of, “Asana is a steady, comfortable posture,” (2.46) 34 but they neglect to include the next sutra, which explains how to practice asana. “By lessening the natural tendency for restlessness and by meditating on the infinite, posture is mastered.” (2.47) 35.

There are a few major takeaways here: First, the key to asana is meditation. Second, Patanjali admits that the mind is naturally restless. So it might be natural to find meditation challenging: It’s in the mind’s nature to constantly move from one thing to another. He is offering asana as a prescription for a busy mind.

It has been revealed that in the very next sutra, Patanjali describes the result of practicing asana: “Thereafter one is undisturbed by the dualities.” (2.48) 36 He’s revealing the truth of asana as a technique for handling the ups and downs of life. Asana not only prepares the body to take a comfortable seat in meditation, it also lifts us above the chaos of life to find a still point of peace.

In a recent development, so many spiritual, and even meditative, practices are conceptual, intellectual, and ethereal. They can feel too subtle to grasp. But the practice of asana is different. It is practical and grounded in its ability to give you access to deeper parts of yourself, whether you have the patience for seated meditation or not.

In a flowing asana series, you can explore the interplay of action and stillness in your body while your mind focuses on each movement. Or you can hold a static posture and notice dynamic inner movement. You can experience the lifting and grounding that you find in the flow of the breath. The inhale bringing in new life, the exhalation letting go; inhale lift, exhale release.

Asana allows you to experience the energy of creation moving through the body and mind. By holding steady, or through movement, stretching, or strengthening, asana clears the subtle energetic pathways and allows your prana to flow.

In a recent development, asana is about expanding your sense of self, yet it’s so often taught in a way that feels limiting or constricting. So many of people struggle with body image, and it’s heartbreaking to think that the way contemporary yoga is taught feeds into this. Instead, yoga can teach you how to cherish your body for giving you this lifetime and for allowing you to engage in spiritual practice. Remember, your body is equally worthy of asana as any other body.

Industry observers note that the body has an essential role in the hatha yoga traditions. It’s perceived as either an obstacle that needs to be overcome, or a vehicle that needs to be strong enough to withstand the force of kundalini, potential prana, flowing through it. Some of the more ascetic, or strictly disciplined, traditions focused on overcoming attachment to the body by forcing it into compliance. These hatha yogis would stand for months on end, hold one arm up in the air, or perform some similarly intense practice. This is a way to force the body into compliance in the hope of releasing attachment to it.

In a recent development, contemporary yoga has maintained a hint of this extreme practice by teaching that the body needs to be whipped into shape in order to be worthy. I don’t think this is a useful idea because it reinforces cultural messages of unworthiness that are used to sell wellness “solutions” back to you. It also feeds the self-hatred and internalized prejudice that flows from ableism, racism, sexism, fat phobia, homophobia, transphobia, ageism, and other kinds of oppression.

You can practice asana as meditation and make movement your practice. You don’t even have to identify as someone who meditates, and you don’t have to sit with your thoughts and feelings. Instead, you can move your body, channel your energy, and find relief from your mind’s ruminations. Your yoga mat or chair is a magic portal to a different land. Take a few breaths, move your body, and then integrate movement with your breath, and poof! Off you go.

Because of the way asana is represented in the media as an extreme sport, it can be intimidating for a lot of people, which is why I’ve spent my entire career teaching people how to make these practices accessible and welcoming. The meditative heart of asana practice is naturally inclusive and accessible. Rather than performing asana or copying what other people do, the question is: Can you listen to your own body? When you practice, let go of your thoughts and focus on how you feel, and what your body needs today.

There are a few different things you can focus on in asana that turns movement into meditation. In fact, you can start by asking yourself what the difference is between asana and exercise. The difference is subtle, and it all comes back to meditation. Is your mind focused when you’re doing asanas? It doesn’t really matter what it’s focused on, but it’s the act of focusing that is key. Mindful awareness is what makes a movement into an asana and into a yoga practice. In the end, you can focus on any of these things:.

According to recent reports, approach a short asana session as a meditation. You can do this with any asana practice focused on your breath. If you have a regular asana practice, do some poses that you enjoy—in a chair or on a yoga mat.

In a recent development, if you are upcoming to asana, consider joining a beginner’s yoga class, or look up chair yoga online. It can be helpful to start in a chair, or even better, a couch. Couch yoga is my favorite way to experience the power of asana as a meditation.

  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property.
  • The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that right now average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

According to recent reports, right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

In a recent development, timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

According to recent reports, ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:.

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most notable financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:.

Industry observers note that rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Recent findings suggest that timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:.

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

According to recent reports, choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

According to recent reports, research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Sources indicate that shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

Sources indicate that A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

It has been revealed that no. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation proposal, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Sources indicate that some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

Recent findings suggest that A timeshare is a prepaid vacation proposal with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

On has come a long way since the days of cobbling together a running shoe from cut pieces of garden hoses and a dream for a springier shoe. Whether you’re a casual road runner or hardcore trail trekker, On wants to match you with one of its pairs.

Once you’re about 15 miles deep, the CloudTec cushioning opens up and the signature CloudTec pods really carry you, giving you an energetic feel and a snappy return. What surprised me the most was how stable the shoe felt in spite of its impressive stack height. Thanks to the relative firmness of the cushioning, I felt surefooted and stable even on uneven surfaces like gravel and rocky terrain.

You can cancel the subscription after the first month (shoes must be unworn and returned within 30 days to get your refund; if you don’t return them you’ll be charged $100).

The Cloud X 4 has an X-shaped Speedboard for forefoot flexion and a midfoot cage for support and lateral stability.

#56770. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1667 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season.
  • One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.
  • With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis).

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

For Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

According to recent reports, he is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

It has been revealed that “I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the substantial mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

Sources indicate that “Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

Sources indicate that “I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

“I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”.

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

According to recent reports, “If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”.

In a recent development, the founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

Sources indicate that “Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”.

Industry observers note that “Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

It has been revealed that “In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”.

It has been revealed that “This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the significant training blocks start.”.

Sources indicate that head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’.

“I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

In a recent development, “For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”.

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the newly introduced technique as you can sustain, and no more.

In a recent development, “You can’t ingrain a latest technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”.

Sources indicate that A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a significant proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

In a recent development, “For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”.

In a recent development, “A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”.

According to recent reports, “Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

Sources indicate that “A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”.

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most vital session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”.

#56769. Breaking: Trek’s Newly introduced Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Trek’s Newly introduced Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, this Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here.
  • According to recent reports, if you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the upcoming Domane belongs on your list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, this Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here. Next, I want to hear what you think. Bicycling members can continue the discussion with me on Discord, where I’ll answer questions and hear how the Domane works for riders beyond my test. The invitation appears after the review.

According to recent reports, if you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the upcoming Domane belongs on your list. It feels more eager under power than previous versions, while keeping the stability and confidence that have always made the bike good at everyday riding.

The version I’d point most people toward is the $4,200 SL 6 AXS. It gets the same geometry, tire clearance, and basic frame features as the expensive SLR models, along with electronic shifting and carbon wheels. The SLR saves weight and opens the door to Trek’s Project One customization. Those are real advantages, but they don’t make it a fundamentally different bike.

It has been revealed that I tested the $11,499 SLR 9 AXS 2x. It weighed 16.3 pounds in size M. The bike I’d recommend first costs less than half as much.

Sources indicate that BIKE TESTED: Trek Gen. 5 Domane SLR 9 AXS 2xACTUAL WEIGHT 16.3 pounds (Size M, as tested) USE Road, light gravel PRICE AS TESTED $11,499 MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,400 to $11,499; $14,999 limited edition ICON No. 76FRAME ONLY OPTION: Yes. $3,700 (SLR) $2,000 (SL)CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS Yes, SLR models through Project One SIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, ML, L, XL WEIGHT LIMIT 125 kg/275 lb (bicycle, rider, and cargo) TIRE CLEARANCE 40mm BB STANDARD T47 threaded BRAKE HOSE ROUTING Internal, RCS headset; under bar/stem on most buildsDRIVETRAIN COMPATIBILITY 1x and 2x, electronic shifting only DERAILLEUR HANGER UDH WARRANTY Lifetime, frame and rigid fork, original owner CRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, Trek Carbon Care discounted replacement.

I’ve ridden every generation of the Domane, including several of the more aggressive RSL versions. Over the years, Trek added adjustable IsoSpeed, front IsoSpeed, internal storage, aero shaping, and hidden cables. The fifth-generation bike pulls back on much of that.

In a recent development, the Gen 5 feels more solid and reactive underfoot than its predecessors. It’s stiffer when I get on the pedals, accelerates with more snap, and climbs with a crispness that used to elude the Domane. In that way, it feels more like a Madone than any previous version.

In a recent development, it hasn’t lost the stability and confidence that make the Domane a good everyday road bike. I can push it hard down a descent without feeling like I’m taking a test of nerves. The fit is excellent, too. The taller front end should help more riders find a position that’s comfortable and aerodynamic.

And no, it doesn’t feel slow on 35mm tires. The bike feels quick and responsive. The wider tires are part of what makes it work, not an anchor holding it back.

In a recent development, the original Domane’s signature feature was IsoSpeed, a mechanism that let the seat tube flex to add comfort. Trek developed it over several generations, then removed it from the bike that introduced it.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh Domane gets much of its comfort from wider tires at lower pressures, along with frame and seatpost tuning. Most models come with 35mm tires, and the frame clears up to 40mm. Trek notes that combination provides enough comfort that IsoSpeed’s remaining benefit isn’t worth its weight and complexity.

IsoSpeed still works. Trek told me that with the same 35mm tires, the Gen 4 transmits slightly less vibrational energy than the Gen 5. Trek also says the Gen 5 on 35mm tires comes within 5 percent of the Gen 4 on its stock 32mm tires at the rear. At the front, Trek says the two generations perform similarly.

Recent findings suggest that those are Trek’s test results, not measurements I made. But the decision makes sense to me. Wider tires add traction and capability that IsoSpeed couldn’t provide. Trek decided the system’s remaining comfort advantage wasn’t enough to justify keeping it.

Recent findings suggest that if you own an older Domane, what did IsoSpeed do for you? Did you notice a difference when you moved to wider tires, or do you miss the old system? I’d like to hear what you’ve felt on real roads.

Sources indicate that according to Trek’s white paper, the Gen 5 frame is about 292 grams lighter than Gen 4. It also eliminates IsoSpeed and its associated maintenance.

Recent findings suggest that the frame uses a threaded T47 bottom bracket, a round fork steerer, a Universal Derailleur Hanger, and a standard 27.2mm seatpost. For a modern performance bike, there’s not much proprietary weirdness here. That’s a feature.

The internal storage compartment is gone, too. I’ll miss it. It was useful. Trek says its research indicated that many Domane owners weren’t using it. The latest frame retains fender mounts, top-tube mounts, and frame-bag mounts. I like the trade: less hardware and complexity, with straightforward ways to carry gear when you need to.

The cable routing is another smart compromise. On most models, brake hoses run beneath the two-piece bar and stem before entering the frame at the headset. It looks clean, but changing a bar or stem doesn’t become a major repair job. Fit changes and service matter more to me than hiding every cable at any cost.

The SL and SLR share the same geometry, tire clearance, seatpost size, bottom bracket, UDH, and general feature set. The SL uses Trek’s 500 Series carbon; the SLR uses lighter 900 Series carbon. Trek says both frames are designed to the same stiffness requirements. The SL supports mechanical drivetrains; the SLR is electronic-shifting only.

The SLR primarily buys lower weight, access to Trek’s highest-end builds, and the ability to customize components through Project One. Buyers can specify details such as crank length, handlebar width, and stem length. If you’re spending this much on a bike, getting those dimensions right from the factory is a meaningful advantage.

According to recent reports, but the SLR doesn’t change the core experience enough to be the obvious choice for most riders. I’d look closely at the $4,200 SL 6 AXS first. It has a carbon frame, electronic shifting, carbon wheels, 40mm tire clearance, and the same accessible fit. The carbon range starts at $2,400 with the Tiagra SL 4. The SLR 9 AXS 2x I tested costs $11,499.

Trek also offers an ultralight SLR 9 AXS 1x with 28mm tires. Trek describes it as the racier interpretation of the Domane, but it did not vibration-test that configuration. If comfort is a big reason you’re considering the bike, pay attention to the tire setup, not just the frame name.

In a recent development, if you’re shopping for a Domane, which versions are you weighing? Would you spend more for the SLR’s lower weight and Project One options, or put that money toward another bike or gear?

It has been revealed that trek indicates it applied aero lessons from the Gen 8 Madone, but aerodynamics weren’t a major priority. In a pedaling-mannequin test, Trek claims the Gen 5 improved by 0.6 watts over Gen 4.

In other words, essentially the same.

According to recent reports, that seems appropriate. Trek prioritized weight, simplicity, and ride quality instead of chasing another aero headline.

The fifth-generation Domane is an excellent road bike. It’s light, comfortable, stable, and lively. It’s easier to adjust and service than many integrated performance bikes, retains useful mounts, and drops features that added weight and complexity without improving the bike enough to justify them.

In a recent development, the old Domanes were more technically adventurous. I miss that part of the story more than I miss riding them.

For most riders, I think Gen 5 is the right Trek road bike. The SL 6 AXS is the model I’d point people toward first. The SLR makes sense if you want the lighter frame and factory customization, but the expensive build doesn’t change the core experience. Taken as a whole, the latest Domane is my favorite drop-bar bike Trek makes.

Recent findings suggest that that’s my take after riding the bike. Now I want to hear from people who own a Domane, have ridden an earlier version, or are considering the Gen 5. What questions do you still have? What would you like me to investigate or compare? I’ll continue the conversation on Discord and bring the most useful questions and experiences back here.

In a recent development, what do you think of the new Trek Domane? What questions do you still have? What did I screw up? If you own or have ridden the Gen 5 Domane, share your impressions.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. #56768. As a Back-of-the-Pack Runner, I Always Struggled to Run at Different Paces—Until I Tried This Approach

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (778 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

As a Back-of-the-Pack Runner, I Always Struggled to Run at Different Paces—Until I Tried This Approach

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app.
  • In a recent development, disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds.
  • Fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app. It included eight one-minute inter­vals interspersed with one minute of recovery. The virtual coach of that run prescribed different speeds, including a mile pace which was “fast,” a 10K pace which was “faster, but slower than a mile pace,” and the slowest of the three, a marathon pace. No matter how much I tried, I couldn’t run at different paces. Over the course of my various flirtations, romances, and relationships with running, I’d always seemed to move at only two speeds: run and walk.

In a recent development, disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds. The name? “Find Your Pace.” Excited about this fortuitous opportunity, I pressed download and started this short workout even though I had just struggled through the previous one.

Fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace. Instead, he only referred to the Rate of Perceived Exertion, a metric that has been around for decades, but that I had, to be honest, ignored for all of that time. RPE is a purely subjective scale from 1 to 10. Typically, 1 refers to an effort level similar to sitting on your couch (i.e., no effort at all), and running at a 3 is a warmup effort. On the other end of the spectrum is 10, an all-out sprint, a pace you can’t sustain for more than half a minute.

It has been revealed that coach Cory explained that my effort level, or exertion, correlated to a variety of distances. For example, I should strive to run a 10K at an RPE of 6, a 5K at 7, and one mile at 9.

Recent findings suggest that he also suggested that runners connect words to different effort levels—for example, the word “strong” when running at the RPE of 6. Honestly, though? At 6, I thought, This is hard, and at 7, I can’t do this. By the time I reached 9, I thought, I have to stop. Coach Cory, on the other hand, suggested I use the word “epic” to describe my fastest pace. He’s clearly an optimist.

According to recent reports, these were very short intervals, so my breathing and heart rate didn’t rise much. But the difference I felt between this run and my previous runs was notable: I was pushing myself in a way I had never done before. I followed Coach Cory’s instructions back and forth on the same block, and not once did I look at my Fitbit or the app to see how fast I was going, which is what I was instructed to do during my previous runs. The whole exercise was over in 10 minutes. You may be thinking, Well, okay, but how fast were you? Did you actually run at different paces?

Industry observers note that turns out, yes, I did. Even more shocking, I had truly picked up speed during these intervals. My mile pace was 9:21, my 5K was 10:30, and my 10K was 10:54. Faster than I’ve ever run during a training run or race. During that one short workout, I realized I could create different paces based on my effort rather than trying to “find” different paces for each race distance.

Industry observers note that I know that might seem like semantics, but the difference is meaningful. “Finding” something isn’t in your control, but “creating” is. When a training strategy listed different goal paces, I couldn’t seem to reach them, but when I ran based on my RPE, I was able to distinguish between different efforts, and those effort levels translated to mile, 5K, and 10K paces.

This run was memorable. It gave me a boost to not give up on myself or my training. It let me know what was possible if I kept training. Now when a race proposal instructs me to run at a 5K or 10K pace, I don’t worry about the speed metrics. Instead, I focus on my effort. Turns out I can create paces even if I can’t find them.

It has been revealed that donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the route of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift was revealed in late October, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a jaunt through central France, and a summit finish atop the Puy de Dôme. The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour will kick off on Friday, July 30, and conclude on Saturday, August 7, after nine days of racing.

In just five editions, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift has become the pinnacle of the women’s WorldTour calendar. And looking at the 2027 route, we’re in for another nine days of aggressive racing, a hard-fought GC battle, and opportunities for a wide range of stage winners. Yet some route choices leave me lukewarm, and a few things are missing altogether. There’s no trek into the Alps or Pyrenees, no individual time trial, and still no Paris finale.

Now, I don’t doubt that the women’s peloton will make the most of the route it’s given, but whether it’ll match the spectacle of previous editions is another question.

First, the highlights, starting with the three-day Grand Départ in England.

In a recent development, the 2027 route puts a lot of the fireworks up front, so there’s no easing into this Tour. It opens with a short, punchy 86km stage from Leeds to Manchester. Officially classified as flat, it still packs in three categorized climbs. So while the sprinters may get their chance at the first yellow jersey, it’s not guaranteed. Then comes a bumpy stage two that, a local tells me, is much harder on the legs than it looks on paper. And then we’ll get the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift’s first team time trial in London.

Leeds, Manchester, London. The 2027 edition will put women’s racing in front of millions. That’s a huge opportunity to draw roadside crowds and reach newly introduced audiences. Those opening stages could also give the GC an intriguing shape. An early winner backed by a strong team performance in London might carry a rider in yellow deep into the race.

Sources indicate that then there’s the Puy de Dôme. The volcano occupies a special place in cycling history, having hosted 14 men’s Tour de France stage finishes, including the famous 1964 head-to-head between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor.

A more recent memory of the Puy de Dôme is that of Matteo Jorgenson’s heartbreak on stage nine of the 2023 Tour. The American attacked alone with almost 50km remaining, only for Canadian Michael Woods to catch and pass him some 450 meters from victory. Jorgenson ultimately finished fourth.

It’s easy to imagine the volcano hosting another exciting chapter in the Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon//SRAM) and Demi Vollering (FDJ United–Suez) rivalry.

According to recent reports, in 2025, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift delivered six different stage winners and three riders in yellow. This year, it was six and five respectively. The 2027 route should again give a broad cast of riders their chance, with plenty of terrain for versatile stage hunters alongside opportunities for the sprinters and climbers.

In a recent development, that’s something I like about the Tour. A Tour stage can define a rider’s season; just look at the breakthrough victories of Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L'Imad), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education–Oatly), and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance–Soudal) in years past.

Recent findings suggest that the route opens the door to well-rounded riders, but the overall will still likely be decided on the final two mountainous days. But if climbing decides the Tour, I’d like to see some high-mountain racing in the Alps or Pyrenees. If the intention is to give more riders a shot at the GC, then I want to believe that they can actually take the yellow home, rather than just borrow it for a few days.

Sources indicate that of course, Vollering and Niewiadoma excel on punchy terrain too. And that’s part of my concern: different profiles don’t guarantee different outcomes. Perhaps the shorter climbs will keep more riders in contention, but I’m not convinced this route broadens the fight for yellow as much as it prolongs it.

Then there’s London. I’m excited about the setting, but the racing format leaves me underwhelmed. I prefer an individual time trial where every rider controls her own performance. No matter the timing rules, a team time trial tends to favor stronger, bigger teams, with more money to spend on a deeper roster, equipment, testing, and optimizing. A rider from a team with fewer resources could leave London with a time loss that reflects her team's budget more than her own performance.

Eighteen kilometers may limit the damage, but as 2024 demonstrated, when Niewiadoma-Phinney won the overall by just four seconds, every single second counts.

Recent findings suggest that while Britain gets the big-city showcases, I feel roadside fans in France get a bad deal. The route bypasses the country’s largest cities on its way to a finale where spectator access remains uncertain.

Strict environmental protections are in place on Puy de Dôme, and organizers are still exploring if they can admit a limited crowd at the summit. I understand the need for protection, but a repeat of 2023’s empty upper slopes would be a lonely way to welcome in the Tour winner. If fans aren’t welcome, surely it’s worth asking whether this is the right place to finish.

Recent findings suggest that and while a summit finish can deliver exciting racing, I’m still waiting to see the women’s peloton finish on the cobblestones of Paris, same as the men. Wout van Aert’s victory in 2025 and Mathieu van der Poel’s all-out effort in 2026 were absolute highlights of those Tours for me. The Montmartre circuit has shown how much racing in Paris can offer, beyond a ceremonial procession. After watching Vollering and Niewiadoma duel in France and again in Montréal, with Marlen Reusser never far behind, I want to see what these women could do on those streets.

#56764. 12 Essential Things I Do In Every Yoga Class I Teach

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1581 w)

12 Essential Things I Do In Every Yoga Class I Teach

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975.
  • Industry observers note that I approached my earliest years of teaching with an enthusiasm that I hope helped make up for my lack of experience.
  • The following points express what I feel are imperatives for yoga teachers to remember while teaching.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about tips for teaching yoga first appeared in the July-August 1997 glitch of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Industry observers note that I approached my earliest years of teaching with an enthusiasm that I hope helped make up for my lack of experience. As I look back now, in my 26th year of teaching, I realize that I have evolved a philosophy that shapes every class I offer. New teachers are usually so busy learning the craft of teaching that articulating a teaching philosophy remains a distant goal. Over time, though, we can evolve a style of teaching that expresses our values.

The following points express what I feel are imperatives for yoga teachers to remember while teaching.

As teachers, what we share with students can have effects that last far beyond the boundaries of class.

The most important condition for a good yoga class is that it become a “sacred circle,” a term coined by author and Jungian psychologist Jean Shinoda Bolen. Each class must be a safe place for the personal exploration of body, emotions, and mind. A good teacher creates this sacred circle in which every student feels valued, respected, and completely safe.

The class must be free from verbal, emotional, physical, and sexual coercion or abuse. Without this intrinsic sense of safety, it is impossible for students to let go and allow the practice to unfold. In this context, safety means that the students retain the right to say no to working with a partner or to being adjusted or touched, and to say yes to moving at their own personal pace.

According to recent reports, look at each person individually and teach to that person in that moment. Each student is an individual to be guided, not a posture to be fixed. Often we focus too much on communicating about a pose instead of with a person. Your students might not remember the details of the asana (pose), but they will remember being seen, heard, and helped.

Humor teaches perspective and reveals your own humanness to students who might otherwise tend to put you on a pedestal. It also enables you to reveal yourself, thus encouraging your students to reveal themselves as well. Laughter improves our breathing by loosening the diaphragm, and helps us to remember that while yoga practice is key, it does not always need to be serious.

I don’t like the word “correct” when applied to teaching an asana since it implies that there is something wrong with the students—that they are less worthy for not “getting it right.”.

“Correcting” and “fixing” a pose sends the unconscious and therefore very powerful message that “it is never enough.” Many of us are already slaves to this judgment. Our houses are never clean enough, our meals never organic enough, our teaching never sophisticated enough. By constantly correcting students, you tell them that, once again, they are not doing enough.

Use your words, images, and very light and occasional touch, if welcomed, to transmit positive information. We need to make sure that students don’t harm themselves, but we also need to communicate that while there is always room to grow, where we are right now has a wholeness and beauty to it.

Sources indicate that are we teaching students to become like piano tuners who never experience the joy of just playing the piano? Do they know volumes about the technique, but nothing about the joy of practicing it? Without proper technique, the benefits of the pose will be lessened and injury can occur. But if technique is all we teach, then there is no heart in our teaching.

In the Yoga Sutras (11:1), Patanjali describes the dual concepts of abhyasa and vairagyam. Abhyasa, or “determined effort,” involves discipline, attention, and action, and it manifests as attention to the form of the posture. Vairagyam, on the other hand, is “supreme detachment.” Vairagyam is surrender, letting go, and allowing; it involves opening to the experience of the practice. When technique and form are balanced with heartfelt, free movement, then the asana is whole.

Sources indicate that learn how to teach the same poses in fresh ways. The basic poses, repeated in almost every class, form the bedrock of teaching. If you are bored with them, change your practice so you can find something new in each pose each time. Also, remember that while you might be bored, your students probably are not.

We all need repetition; it is really the only way we learn anything. If you have taught for some time, no doubt you have had more than one student come to you in amazement to report a “great insight” about a pose he or she just learned from another teacher. You might have been teaching this concept for years, but suddenly the student was ready to hear it.

Even as you repeat familiar poses, include something newly introduced in each class. It need not be a difficult posture or technique. It can be as simple as a new way to practice Savasana, but it will nonetheless keep your classes fresh.

“Listen” means observing with all your senses, as well as with your heart. Then teach from your heart what the students need right now. Do not be limited by what you think you “should” teach.

No matter how much training you have or how many years you have been teaching, each class is a newly introduced experience. Trust your intuition about what is appropriate in this moment and teach that.

For a couple of weeks after the San Francisco earthquake in 1989, my students found it almost impossible to practice standing poses. No one trusted the earth. Each time I would try to teach standing poses, students would have balance problems and become agitated. We all needed the reassurance of sitting down for a while. I responded to this obvious problem by focusing on seated poses, gradually reintroducing standing poses as it seemed appropriate.

In a recent development, the body is programmed to move according to complex neurological and muscular patterns involving whole groups of muscles. We spend a great deal of teaching time trying to use words to isolate specific movements, when actually that is not how the body learns and remembers.

Recent findings suggest that when children learn a movement, they practice and experiment until they learn the muscle pattern which accomplishes that movement. Imagine trying to tell someone how to walk—explaining exactly which muscles to use as agonists, which as antagonists, and which as stabilizers. Walking is too complex an activity for someone to talk you through it.

Nevertheless, teachers are stuck with using words until the student understands a movement from within. So choose your words carefully. “Invite,” “entice,” and “allow” have a very different feeling than “push,” “tighten,” “stamp,” “grind,” and “cut.” In a recent class I suggested that students “conjure” the pose out of their bodies. Images such as these help the student bypass the linear left brain and access the right brain, where whole movements are understood.

Recent findings suggest that try focusing on one thing in each asana rather than loading the student down with information. In the information age, we are overburdened with facts. We can know everything about the pose and still be unhappy in our lives. While knowledge about the pose can be useful and even necessary, it will not provide us with what we all crave: peace of mind, clarity, and compassion.

Allow the experience of the pose to be the true teacher—not your words.

Let the last part of the class be simpler and the sequence will be more satisfying. Sometimes it helps to have a theme—a part of the body, for example—to focus on in every pose. Whatever you choose, allow the instructions to become simpler as the students slow down and internalize their awareness.

Sleep-deprived Americans desperately need rest. Give your students the gift of learning how to relax at will by lying down on the floor in relaxation pose. I never cease to be amazed to hear from students that Savasana was skipped in another class and labeled unimportant. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Studies document that relaxation lowers blood pressure and other physiological parameters associated with stress, including respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and brain waves. Relaxation measurably improves the function of the immune system.

Savasana teaches much more than relaxation. It teaches clearly and concretely the importance of being, not just doing. Our culture is very much a “doing” culture; we value action and results over being and awareness. Savasana might be the only time during the week that the student is quiet and present—not acting, not achieving, not sleeping. This is the beginning of meditation and an extremely important gift. Always allow 20 minutes for deep relaxation. [Editor’s Note: This article was written in 1997. We support a long Savasana! And it’s okay if you can’t allow 20 minutes for Savasana.].

The integrity of a teacher’s practice expresses itself in several ways. First and foremost, it reflects how the teacher lives his or her life. Honesty in living makes possible honesty in teaching. A teacher’s formal yoga practice should be regular, not haphazard. But most key, this practice should include love for yourself and your students, as well as love of yoga and life itself.
